description:
Chinaberry (Melia azedarach)

23 July 2016
Greenbelt Park 428
Denton County, Texas

A single and still small Chinaberry tree grew in the shaded canopy by the side of the trail with its characteristic trunk, leaves and spring flowers now turned into the green berries of midsummer. Chinaberry is considered an invasive tree in the United States and goes by several common names in English including Pride of India, Bead-tree, Cape Lilac, Syringa Berrytree, Persian Lilac, and Indian Lilac. It is original to the Himalayas according to one source and generally to the "Indomalaya and Australasia" regions of the world and is related to the mahogany family of trees. It is considered to be a fast-growing tree that will affect native species by changing the pH balance of the soil underneath it. It was introduced to the US in the mid-1800s, according to the Texas Invasives online site. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department administers Greenbelt Park 428.

The fruit of the White Cedar is round (1.5cm in diameter), fleshy and yellow in colour when mature. Fruits are poisonous to humans and some other mammals but birds are able to eat the fruits and thus disperse the seed through their droppings. Some reports suggest that 6-8 fruits can be fatal to humans.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; Day 2 of our 3-day Thanksgiving holiday trip to the eastern Panhandle.

Our itinerary for Day 2 was:

0655-1008 CST: Chipola River Water Management Area (Calhoun County; return trip from yesterday)

1016-1118 CST: Altha (Calhoun County)

1122-1153 CST: Mount Olive Cemetery Road (Calhoun County)

1245-1304 CST: lunch at the Blountstown Subway (Calhoun County)

1335-1343 CST: Willis Bridge Park (Calhoun County; 1 species!)

1400-1506 CST: Chipola River Boat Ramp (Calhoun County)

1615-1708 CST: Sam Atkins Park (Calhoun County; we got rained out)

1845 CST: we checked into the Apalachicola Bay Inn (Franklin County). We ate at a rather pricey restaurant in Apalachicola, where all food was served in Styrofoam containers and plasticware, which was all thrown into the trash when we were finished; weird.

We barely saw the sun on any of the three days; most photographs were taken under gloomy skies, which meant that I often had to boost the light saturation to get a usable image, even if the image ended up looking washed-out.

The weather at this spot was cloudy, 71 degrees, and breezy. We left at 1118 CST.

Val and I have set a goal of attaining 50 or more bird species in each of Florida's 67 counties (Val has reached or exceeded this total in 57 counties, while I have reached or exceeded 50 species in 56 counties). Calhoun County was our primary target this trip; we each started the trip with 14 species. Owing to Val's much-better hearing than mine, Val ended this day with 51 species, while I ended up with 45.

Construction has undermined the trees, wildflowers, most of the grass and so forth, the biodiversity once found at the site. Bulldozers, caterpillars, and other earth-moving equipment obeying the grand scheme of things effectively saw to that. There once was a small wetlands at the location in part fed by a trickle of a stream that had survived until recently.
